idea.title: Why a comet's tail points away from the Sun
idea.description: The tail is not a wake: what pushes it.

shots.visual: a comet moving away from the Sun, tail ahead
shots.narration: In this video: comet tails point away from the Sun because sunlight pushes the dust and the solar wind, found by Biermann in 1951, pushes the gas.
shots.shows: the tail leads the comet outward

shots.visual: the same stream reaching Earth, a city's lights going out
shots.narration: A tail that leads? The thing pushing it reaches you too. In March 1989 a storm in it put Quebec's power out for nine hours.
shots.shows: the stream that bends the tail arrives at Earth

shots.narration: Sunlight pushes. Not much, but on a grain of dust it is enough.

shots.visual: a straight gas tail beside a curved dust tail
shots.narration: But a comet has a second tail, of gas, and it is straight and fast. Far too fast for sunlight alone.
shots.shows: the gas tail outruns the dust tail

shots.visual: the two tails, the straight one highlighted
shots.narration: In 1951 Ludwig Biermann asked the obvious question: what else is blowing?

shots.visual: particles streaming out from the Sun past a comet
shots.narration: His answer: the Sun never stops shedding itself. A stream of particles pours out of it, in every direction, all the time.
shots.shows: particles leaving the Sun and bending the gas tail

shots.narration: Eleven years later Mariner 2 flew through it and measured it. We call it the solar wind.
So look again at that comet.

shots.visual: the opening comet, the stream visible
shots.narration: It is not flying backwards. It is showing you the wind.
shots.shows: the tail pointing along the stream
